questions.q: A PostgreSQL server listens on a network port. Which port is the default?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL uses port 5432 unless you choose another. 3000 and 8080 are typical for your own web servers, and 443 is HTTPS.

questions.q: In Docker, what is the difference between an image and a container?
questions.explain: docker pull postgres:17 downloads the image. docker run starts a container from it. You can run several containers from one image.
options: They are two names for the same thing
An image is the packaged program; a container is one running copy of it
A container is the download; an image is the running program
An image holds your data; a container holds the program

questions.q: What does -p 5434:5432 mean in docker run ... -p 5434:5432 ... postgres:17?
questions.explain: The left number is on your computer (the host), the right one inside the container. You then connect with psql -p 5434.
options: Port 5434 on your computer connects to port 5432 inside the container
Port 5432 on your computer connects to port 5434 inside the container
The container may use any port from 5432 to 5434
PostgreSQL 17 runs on port 5434 inside the container

questions.q: docker run ... -p 5432:5432 ... fails with address already in use. What does the lesson do?
questions.explain: Another program already uses 5432 on this computer. Docker created the container anyway, so docker rm pg frees the name pg. Then a different left number avoids the clash.
options: Stops Docker and reinstalls it
Runs the same command again until it works
Removes the failed container with docker rm pg and runs it again on another host port, such as 5434
Changes PostgreSQL's port inside the container to 5434

questions.q: How does the lesson set the password for the postgres user in Docker?
questions.explain: A made-up password typed into commands ends up in notes, chats and shell history. A random value in an environment variable stays out of the command text, and psql reads PGPASSWORD by itself.
options: It types a simple password like postgres into the command
It leaves the password empty, because the server only runs locally
It generates a random password into the PGPASSWORD environment variable and passes it with -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD="$PGPASSWORD"
It saves the password in package.json

questions.q: What happens to the database's data when you run docker stop pg and later docker rm pg?
questions.explain: A stopped container still exists with its data. Removing it deletes the data with it. docker rmi additionally deletes the downloaded image.
options: stop deletes the data; rm only deletes the name
stop keeps the data (docker start pg brings it back); rm deletes the container and its data
Both keep the data forever
Both delete the data

questions.q: In psql, which command connects you to the database taskdb?
questions.explain: Lines starting with a backslash are psql's own commands. \c connects, and the prompt changes to taskdb=#.
options: use taskdb;
\c taskdb
\dt taskdb
connect taskdb;

questions.q: You are connected with psql. Which command lists the tables, and which describes the tasks table?
questions.explain: \dt lists tables, and \d tasks shows the columns, types, defaults and indexes of one table. \q quits.
options: \q lists them; \c tasks describes it
show tables; lists them; describe tasks; describes it
\dt lists them; \d tasks describes it
\d lists them; \dt tasks describes it

questions.q: In psql you type select * from tasks and press Enter, but nothing happens and the prompt changes. Why?
questions.explain: psql runs a statement when it sees the ;. Type ; and press Enter. Backslash commands like \dt need no semicolon.
options: The table is empty
SQL lines end with ;, so psql is waiting for the rest of the statement
psql only accepts SQL in capital letters
You must start every SQL line with a backslash

questions.q: What does create database taskdb; do?
questions.explain: One server can hold one database per project, for example. After creating it, connect with \c taskdb and create tables inside it.
options: Starts a second PostgreSQL server
Makes a new, empty database on the same server; one server can hold many
Creates a table called taskdb
Makes a backup of the current database

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: returning * gives back the whole new row, including the id the database chose and the default values. It is exactly what a POST /tasks handler needs for its 201 answer.
options: { id: 3, user_id: 2, title: 'Fix bike', done: false, priority: 2 }
{ id: 1, user_id: 2, title: 'Fix bike', done: false, priority: 2 }
{ user_id: 2, title: 'Fix bike' }
undefined

questions.q: Why add returning * to an insert in a POST /tasks handler?
questions.explain: The handler must answer 201 with the new task. returning gives it back in the same round trip, including values the database filled in.
options: It makes the insert safe from SQL injection
It returns the new row, with its generated id, without a second query
It undoes the insert if it fails
It is required, or the row is not saved

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Task 1 is done and task 4 belongs to user 2, so both are filtered out. The rest sort by priority (1, 1, 3), and the id breaks the tie between tasks 2 and 5.

questions.q: A query has no order by. In which order do the rows come back?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL returns rows in whatever order it finds them. The lesson's delete ... returning came back as 1, 5, 2 because row 2 had just been updated.
options: Always sorted by the primary key
Always in the order they were inserted
No order is guaranteed; only order by promises one
Alphabetically by the first text column

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: % means "any characters". like is case-sensitive, so it finds only "Fix bike" and "Read book". ilike ignores case and also finds "Buy milk".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: offset 3 skips three rows, and limit 3 takes at most three: page 2 with three tasks per page, the same offset pagination as the REST lesson.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In SQL, null is not equal to anything, not even to null, so = null matches no row. Test for a missing value with is null.

questions.q: How do you write the text value Buy milk directly in SQL (for example, in psql)?
questions.explain: SQL text values use single quotes. Double quotes mean something else in PostgreSQL: a name, such as a column name. In your programs, pass values with placeholders instead.
options: "Buy milk"
'Buy milk'
`Buy milk`
Buy milk without quotes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Task 3 exists, but it belongs to user 2, so the where matches nothing for user 1. affectedRows is 0, and the handler answers 404: the task does not exist for this user.

questions.q: Why does every query in a real API include user_id = $n in its where?
questions.explain: Ids are easy to guess (1, 2, 3, …). Scoping every query to the logged-in user means a guessed id from someone else matches no row.
options: To make the query faster
Because PostgreSQL requires a second condition
Without it, a user could read or change another user's task just by guessing its id
So that returning works

questions.q: update tasks set done = true where id = $1 and user_id = $2 reports affectedRows 0. What should the PATCH /tasks/:id handler answer?
questions.explain: Nothing matched: the task does not exist for this user. A 404 also avoids telling a stranger that a task with that id exists for somebody else.
options: 200 with the unchanged task
403 Forbidden, saying the task belongs to someone else
404 Not Found
500, because the query failed

questions.q: Someone forgot the where. What does this print?
questions.explain: An update or delete without where is valid SQL and changes every row. Write the where first, and in psql run it as a select to check what it matches.
options: error: update requires a where clause

questions.q: You are about to run a delete in psql on a real database. What habit does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: delete from tasks; deletes everything. Checking the where with a harmless select shows exactly which rows the delete would hit.
options: Run it without where first to see how many rows exist
Run the same where as a select first and look at what it matches
Always add limit 1 to the delete
Write the statement in capital letters so it is easier to read

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The where matches the two done tasks. returning id gives back the deleted rows, and two tasks are left.

questions.q: This code glues input into SQL text. What SQL does it build?
questions.explain: The quote in the input closes the SQL text value early, and the rest becomes part of the query. Template literals do no escaping at all.
options: select * from tasks where user_id = 1 and title = 'x' or '1'='1'
select * from tasks where user_id = 1 and title = 'x\' or \'1\'=\'1'
select * from tasks where user_id = 1 and title = "x' or '1'='1"
select * from tasks where user_id = 1 and title = ''

questions.q: Insecure code, shown to understand the attack. What does this print?
questions.explain: and is evaluated before or, and '1'='1' is always true, so the condition matches every row. User 1 just read user 2's tasks. This is SQL injection.

questions.q: The same attack, now with placeholders. What does this print?
questions.explain: The SQL text and the values travel separately, so the input can never become part of the query. It is just a strange title that no task has.
options: error: syntax error at or near "or"

questions.q: Why do $1 placeholders stop SQL injection?
questions.explain: Placeholders do not clean anything. The database parses the SQL first and only then plugs the values in as data, whatever characters they contain.
options: They remove quotes from the input
They check the input against a list of known attacks
The SQL text and the values reach the database separately, so a value can never become part of the SQL
They turn every value into a number

questions.q: The client sends ?sort=title. How do you use it in order by safely?
questions.explain: Placeholders work only for values, not for column names or asc/desc. For names, choose from a fixed list in your code.
options: order by $1 with [sort] as the values
Paste it in: `order by ${sort}`, after removing quotes
Pick the column name from an allow-list in your code, such as { title: "title", id: "id" }, and never paste the client's text
Wrap it in single quotes: `order by '${sort}'`

questions.q: Which query is the safe one? title and sort come from the client.
questions.explain: Only the placeholder version is safe. Pasting sort is injectable, and cleaning input by hand fails sooner or later (and breaks titles like Ada's book).
options: db.query(`select * from tasks order by ${sort}`)
db.query("select * from tasks where title = $1", [title])
db.query("select * from tasks where title = '" + title.replaceAll("'", "") + "'")
db.query(`select * from tasks where title = '${title}'`)

questions.q: db.query("select * from tasks where id = " + Number(id)) happens to be safe today. Why does the lesson still reject it?
questions.explain: Safety should not depend on one easy-to-miss function call. With $1, the query stays safe whatever changes around it.
options: Because Number can return a string
It is fragile: the next person edits it, drops Number, and it becomes injectable
Because ids must always be text
Because PostgreSQL cannot compare numbers

questions.q: Finish insertTask(userId, title). It returns a parameterized query object { text, values }: the SQL inserts into tasks (user_id, title) using $1 and $2, and returns the whole new row.
questions.explain: The SQL text never changes, whatever the title is. The dangerous-looking title is only a value in the values array, so it is stored as plain text. You would run it as db.query(q.text, q.values).

questions.q: Finish findTasks(userId, filters). Always filter by user_id. Add done = $n when filters.done is a boolean, and title ilike $n (with % around the text) when filters.q is set. Number the placeholders in order, join the conditions with and, and end with order by id. Return { text, values }.
questions.explain: Only fixed SQL fragments go into the text; every client value goes into values. The placeholder number is the value's position, so push first, then use values.length.

questions.q: Finish orderBy(sort). sort is the client's text, such as "title" or "-createdAt" (leading minus means descending). Map the names with COLUMNS, and return the SQL fragment with id as a tie-breaker, e.g. order by created_at desc, id. For an unknown name, return null.
questions.explain: Placeholders cannot stand for column names, so the column comes from your own allow-list. The client's text only chooses an entry; it is never pasted. Object.hasOwn avoids matching inherited names like toString.
questions.expected:
order by title, id
order by created_at desc, id
null

questions.q: Finish pageQuery(userId, page, perPage) for offset pagination. Pages start at 1. Return { text, values } for select id, title from tasks where user_id = $1 order by id limit $2 offset $3 with the right values.
questions.explain: Page 1 skips nothing; page 3 with 10 per page skips 20 rows. limit and offset accept placeholders too, because they are values.

questions.q: Finish updateTask(userId, id, changes). Only the fields title and done may change; ignore any other key. Build update tasks set … where id = $n and user_id = $m returning * with numbered placeholders, and return { text, values }.
questions.explain: Loop over your list of allowed fields, not over the client's keys. The attempt to move the task to user 2 is simply ignored, and user_id in the where keeps the update scoped to its owner.

questions.q: Finish insertMany(userId, titles): one insert for several rows. Each row is ($a, $b) with the user id and a title, rows separated by , . Return { text, values }.
questions.explain: Several rows can go in one insert, separated by commas. The placeholders keep counting across rows, and the values stay in one flat array in the same order.
questions.expected:
insert into tasks (user_id, title) values ($1, $2), ($3, $4), ($5, $6)
[ 1, 'Buy milk', 1, 'Call Ada', 1, 'Fix bike' ]

questions.q: This in-memory store behaves like the lesson's completeTask. Finish it: find the task with this id and this userId, set done to true and return it; if there is none, return null.
questions.explain: Match on the id and the owner, just like where id = $1 and user_id = $2. Someone else's task and a missing task look the same (null, then 404), so nothing leaks.

questions.q: What do the flags in psql -h localhost -p 5434 -U postgres mean?
questions.explain: The password is not a flag: psql reads it from the PGPASSWORD environment variable, so it never appears in the command text.
options: -h is the host, -p the port, -U the user
-h shows help, -p is the password, -U is the URL
-h is the host, -p the password, -U the user
-h is the history file, -p the port, -U the update mode

questions.q: You set PGPASSWORD with export in one terminal window, then open a new window and run psql. What happens?
questions.explain: An environment variable set with export (or $env: in PowerShell) only lives in that terminal window and the programs it starts.
options: psql finds the password, because export saves it for the whole computer
The variable is not set in the new window, so you must set it again there
psql reads the password from the Docker container
The new window deletes the database

questions.q: Someone tries to make input "safe" by removing quotes. What does this print?
questions.explain: Cleaning by hand breaks real data: the task is called Ada's book, so this finds nothing. And sooner or later an attacker finds a trick the cleaning missed. Use a placeholder instead.
options: select * from tasks where title = 'Adas book'
select * from tasks where title = 'Ada's book'
select * from tasks where title = 'Ada\'s book'
select * from tasks where title = $1

questions.q: A query builder numbers its placeholders like this. What does it print?
questions.explain: Each placeholder number is the position of its value in the array. Pushing the value first and then using values.length keeps them in step. The values themselves never enter the SQL text.
options: user_id = $1 and done = $2 and priority = $3 [ 1, false, 3 ]
user_id = $1 and done = $1 and priority = $1 [ 1, false, 3 ]
user_id = $1 and done = false and priority = 3 [ 1 ]
user_id = $1 and done = $3 and priority = $2 [ 1, false, 3 ]

questions.q: An attacker's input turns the condition into user_id = 1 and title = 'x' or '1'='1'. Why does it match every row?
questions.explain: It reads as (user_id = 1 and title = 'x') or ('1'='1'). The right side is always true, so every row matches, including other users' rows.
options: Because or is evaluated before and
Because and is evaluated first, and ... or '1'='1' is then always true
Because PostgreSQL ignores the user_id column
Because text in single quotes always equals true
